lessons.title: Identifying fresh cassava roots in local markets
lessons.body: When you buy cassava roots at the market, you need to pick ones that are fresh and good for baking. Fresh cassava roots are firm and hard. Press the root with your thumb; it should not leave a dent. The skin should be brown and rough, with no soft spots or mould. Avoid roots that are wet or have a sour smell. A fresh root snaps cleanly when you break it. The inside should be white or creamy white, with no black lines or discoloration. If you see black streaks, the root is old or diseased. Size matters: medium-sized roots, about 2 to 3 inches in diameter, are best. Very thick roots can be woody and fibrous. Also, look at the ends: they should be clean and dry, not mushy. In many African markets, cassava is sold in piles. Ask the seller to cut a small piece for you to check. If the inside is white and smells fresh, it's good. If it smells like almonds (bitter) or is yellowish, reject it. Buy cassava that was harvested recently, ideally within 2 days. In hot weather, cassava spoils fast. So, buy from a seller who has a fresh supply. If you can, buy directly from a farmer. You can also test by scratching the skin: fresh cassava skin is hard to scratch, while old cassava skin peels off easily. Another trick: fresh cassava is heavy for its size. Pick up two roots of the same size; the heavier one has more water and is fresher. After buying, use it within 2 to 3 days. If you must store it, keep it in a cool, dark place. Remember, cassava that is not fresh will give you poor-quality flour and bread. So, take your time to choose well.

lessons.title: Understanding sweet vs bitter cassava varieties
lessons.body: Cassava comes in two main types: sweet and bitter. The difference is in the amount of cyanide, a natural poison. Sweet cassava has low cyanide and can be eaten after peeling and cooking. Bitter cassava has high cyanide and must be processed carefully to remove the poison. In Africa, sweet cassava is often eaten boiled or fried, while bitter cassava is used for flour, gari, and fufu. For baking, you can use both, but you must process bitter cassava properly to make it safe. How to tell them apart? Sweet cassava roots usually have a light brown skin and white flesh. They taste slightly sweet when raw. Bitter cassava roots often have a darker skin and yellow or creamy flesh. They taste very bitter and leave a burning sensation in your mouth. Never taste raw bitter cassava to check; it can be dangerous. Instead, ask the seller or farmer. They know their varieties. Common sweet varieties in Africa include 'TME 419' and 'TMS 30572'. Bitter varieties include 'TMS 91/02324' and 'TMS 92/0326'. If you are not sure, treat it as bitter and process it well. For baking, sweet cassava is easier because you can peel, wash, and grate it directly. Bitter cassava needs extra steps: soaking, pressing, and fermenting to remove cyanide. The cyanide is in the water, so you must squeeze it out. A simple test: grate a small piece, squeeze the juice, and put a drop on a piece of paper. If it turns blue with a cyanide test kit (available at some agro-shops), it's bitter. But most home bakers don't have kits. So, rely on local knowledge. In many villages, people know which variety is sweet or bitter. Always ask. If you use bitter cassava without proper processing, you can get sick. So, choose sweet cassava for simple baking, or learn to process bitter cassava safely.

lessons.title: How to peel and wash cassava safely
lessons.body: Peeling cassava is simple, but you must do it safely because the raw root contains cyanide. Start by cutting off both ends of the root with a sharp knife. Then, make a shallow cut along the length of the root, through the skin only. Use your thumb to lift the skin and peel it off. If the skin is thick, use a knife to help. Work on a clean surface, like a wooden board or a mat. Wear gloves if you have them, because the raw juice can irritate your skin. If you don't have gloves, wash your hands with soap after peeling. Never touch your eyes or mouth while peeling. After peeling, cut the root into smaller pieces, about 2 to 3 inches long. Remove any woody core or black spots. Then, wash the pieces in plenty of clean water. Use a large bowl or basin. Rub the pieces with your hands to remove dirt and starch. Change the water at least twice. The water will become milky white. That's the starch. For sweet cassava, you can now grate or boil it. For bitter cassava, you must soak the pieces in water for 24 to 48 hours, changing the water every 6 hours. This removes cyanide. After soaking, drain and squeeze the pieces to remove excess water. You can use a clean cloth or a sieve. Then, wash again with clean water. Always wash your hands, knives, and boards with soap and hot water after handling raw cassava. Do not let children or animals eat the peelings. Dispose of peelings in a pit or burn them. If you feel dizzy or sick while peeling, stop and get fresh air. Cyanide gas can be released when peeling bitter cassava. So, work in a well-ventilated area, like outside or near an open window. With practice, peeling 5 kg of cassava takes about 30 minutes. Stay safe and clean.

lessons.title: Tools needed for cassava processing on a budget
lessons.body: You don't need expensive machines to start processing cassava for baking. With a few basic tools, you can do everything by hand. First, a sharp knife. A kitchen knife or machete works. Keep it sharp to peel easily. Second, a cutting board or a clean flat stone. Third, a large bowl or basin for washing. Plastic basins are cheap and available in any market. Fourth, a grater. You can use a traditional hand grater, or make one by punching holes in a tin can. But a proper box grater is better. In many African markets, you can buy a cassava grater for a low price. Fifth, a clean cloth or a mesh bag for squeezing. A strong cotton cloth works well. Sixth, a sieve or a basket for draining. Seventh, a drying tray. You can use a clean mat, a wooden board, or a metal sheet. For drying in the sun, a raised platform keeps it clean. Eighth, a mortar and pestle for pounding if you want flour. Or you can take your dried cassava to a local mill. Ninth, a scale for measuring. A simple kitchen scale is fine. Tenth, storage containers. Use airtight jars or plastic buckets with lids. For fermenting bitter cassava, you need a large pot or bucket with a lid. For pressing, you can use a simple wooden press made from two boards and a rope, or just use heavy stones. All these tools can be found locally or made by a carpenter or welder. You don't need electricity. Start small: a knife, basin, grater, and cloth are enough to make cassava flour for your family or small bakery. As your business grows, you can invest in a motorized grater or a hydraulic press. But for now, keep it simple and cheap. Clean your tools after every use to avoid contamination.

lessons.title: Storing fresh cassava to avoid spoilage
lessons.body: Fresh cassava roots spoil quickly, often within 2 to 3 days after harvest. To avoid spoilage, you must store them properly. The best way is to use them immediately. But if you must store, keep them in a cool, dark, and dry place. Do not leave them in the sun. In hot African climates, cassava can rot in one day if left outside. One method is to bury the roots in slightly moist sand or soil. This keeps them fresh for up to one week. Use a shaded area, like under a tree or in a shed. Another method is to wrap the roots in dry banana leaves or newspaper and keep them in a basket. This works for 3 to 4 days. Do not wash the roots before storing; washing removes the natural protective layer and speeds up spoilage. Only wash just before peeling. If you have a refrigerator, you can store peeled cassava in a plastic bag in the vegetable compartment for up to 5 days. But many bakers don't have fridges. Another option is to process the cassava into flour or dough and store that instead. Dried cassava flour can last for 6 months in an airtight container. To dry, grate or slice the cassava and sun-dry for 2 to 3 days until brittle. Then mill and store. For fresh roots, check them daily. Remove any that show mould or soft spots. One bad root can spoil the others. So, sort them regularly. If you buy in bulk, only buy what you can use in 3 days. In markets, cassava is often sold in large bundles. If you buy a bundle, share with other bakers or process it quickly. You can also freeze grated cassava. Squeeze out excess water, pack in plastic bags, and freeze. It lasts for 3 months. Thaw before use. Remember, spoilage is the biggest loss for cassava bakers. So, plan your purchases and storage carefully.

lessons.title: Health and safety when handling raw cassava
lessons.body: Raw cassava contains cyanide, a poison. Sweet cassava has small amounts, but bitter cassava has a lot. You must handle it safely to avoid getting sick. The first rule: never eat raw cassava. Always peel, wash, and cook or process it. The cyanide is in the juice. So, when you peel or grate, do it in a well-ventilated area. Open windows or work outside. Cyanide gas can be released, especially from bitter cassava. If you feel dizzy, headache, or nausea, stop and move to fresh air. Wear gloves if possible. If you don't have gloves, wash your hands with soap and water immediately after handling. Do not touch your face, eyes, or mouth with unwashed hands. Keep children away from raw cassava and peelings. Do not let animals eat the peelings; they can get sick too. Dispose of peelings by burning or burying deep. For bitter cassava, you must remove cyanide by soaking, fermenting, and pressing. Soak grated or sliced cassava in water for 24 to 48 hours, changing water every 6 hours. Then squeeze out all the water. The cyanide goes into the water. After processing, cook the cassava thoroughly. Boiling, frying, or baking destroys any remaining cyanide. If you are making flour, ensure the cassava is completely dried and milled. Dry it in the sun for 2 to 3 days. A simple test for cyanide: take a small piece of processed cassava and smell it. If it smells like bitter almonds, it may still have cyanide. Cook it more. Never skip the processing steps for bitter cassava. Also, keep your work area clean. Wash knives, boards, and bowls with soap and hot water. Do not use the same cloth for raw cassava and other foods. If you feel sick after handling cassava, drink plenty of water and seek medical help. Prevention is easy: follow the steps, and you will be safe.

quiz.q: What is the best way to check if a cassava root is fresh at the market?
options: A) Press it with your thumb; it should be firm
B) Smell it; it should have a sour smell
C) Look for soft spots and mould
D) Shake it; it should rattle
quiz.explanation: Fresh cassava is firm and hard, so pressing with your thumb should not leave a dent.

quiz.q: Which part of the cassava root should be white or creamy white when you break it?
quiz.explanation: Fresh cassava should have white or creamy white flesh inside, with no black lines.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid cassava roots with black streaks inside?
options: B) They are old or diseased
D) They are hard to peel
quiz.explanation: Black streaks indicate the root is old or diseased and not suitable for baking.

quiz.q: What size of cassava roots is best for baking?
options: C) Medium-sized roots about 2-3 inches in diameter
quiz.explanation: Medium-sized roots are best because very thick roots can be woody and fibrous.

quiz.q: How soon should you use fresh cassava after buying it?
quiz.explanation: Fresh cassava spoils quickly, so it should be used within 2-3 days.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between sweet and bitter cassava?
quiz.explanation: Sweet cassava has low cyanide, while bitter cassava has high cyanide.

quiz.q: Which cassava variety is safer to eat after just peeling and cooking?
quiz.explanation: Sweet cassava has low cyanide and can be eaten after peeling and cooking.

quiz.q: How can you tell if a cassava root is bitter without tasting it?
options: A) It has a darker skin and yellow flesh
C) It has a sweet smell
quiz.explanation: Bitter cassava often has darker skin and yellow or creamy flesh, and tastes bitter.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are not sure whether cassava is sweet or bitter?
options: A) Taste a small piece raw
B) Treat it as bitter and process it well
quiz.explanation: If unsure, treat it as bitter and process it to remove cyanide safely.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common sweet cassava variety in Africa?
quiz.explanation: TME 419 is a common sweet cassava variety, while the others are often bitter.

quiz.q: What is the first step in peeling cassava?
quiz.explanation: Cutting off both ends makes it easier to peel the cassava root.

quiz.q: Why should you wear gloves when peeling raw cassava?
options: A) To keep your hands warm
B) To avoid skin irritation from the juice
D) To prevent the cassava from turning black
quiz.explanation: The raw juice can irritate your skin, so gloves protect your hands.

quiz.q: How long should you soak bitter cassava to remove cyanide?
quiz.explanation: Soaking for 24-48 hours, changing water every 6 hours, helps remove cyanide.

quiz.q: What should you do with cassava peelings after peeling?
options: B) Throw them in the garden
C) Burn or bury them deep
quiz.explanation: Peelings contain cyanide, so they should be burned or buried deep to prevent harm.

quiz.q: Why is it important to work in a well-ventilated area when peeling bitter cassava?
options: B) To prevent cyanide gas buildup
C) To keep the cassava cool
D) To dry the cassava faster
quiz.explanation: Cyanide gas can be released, so good ventilation prevents inhalation.

quiz.q: Which tool can you use as a cheap grater for cassava?
options: A) A tin can with punched holes
quiz.explanation: A tin can with punched holes can be used as a makeshift grater.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a clean cloth or mesh bag in cassava processing?
options: B) To squeeze out excess water
quiz.explanation: A cloth or mesh bag is used to squeeze out excess water from grated cassava.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a basic tool needed for cassava processing on a budget?
quiz.explanation: An electric blender is not necessary; manual tools like a knife, bowl, and grater are enough.

quiz.q: How can you make a simple press for cassava at home?
options: A) Use two boards and a rope
quiz.explanation: All these methods can be used to press cassava and remove water.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store fresh cassava roots to avoid spoilage?
options: A) Leave them in the sun
B) Bury them in moist sand
C) Wash them and keep in fridge
D) Wrap in plastic and keep warm
quiz.explanation: Burying in moist sand in a shaded area keeps cassava fresh for up to a week.

quiz.q: Why should you not wash cassava roots before storing them?
options: A) It makes them too wet
B) It removes the natural protective layer
quiz.explanation: Washing removes the natural protective layer, speeding up spoilage.

quiz.q: How long can dried cassava flour last if stored in an airtight container?
quiz.explanation: Dried cassava flour can last for about 6 months in an airtight container.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see mould on one cassava root in storage?
options: A) Cut off the mouldy part and use the rest
B) Remove it immediately to prevent spoilage of others
D) Leave it with the others
quiz.explanation: One bad root can spoil the others, so remove it immediately.

quiz.q: How can you store grated cassava for a longer time?
options: B) Freeze it in plastic bags
C) Dry it in the sun
D) Leave it at room temperature
quiz.explanation: Freezing grated cassava after squeezing out water can last for 3 months.

quiz.q: What is the first rule of handling raw cassava?
options: B) Always cook it with salt
D) Peel it under running water
quiz.explanation: Raw cassava contains cyanide, so it must never be eaten raw.

quiz.q: What should you do if you feel dizzy while peeling bitter cassava?
options: C) Move to fresh air and stop
quiz.explanation: Dizziness may be from cyanide gas; move to fresh air and stop working.

quiz.q: How can you test if processed cassava still has cyanide?
options: B) Smell it for bitter almonds
quiz.explanation: A bitter almond smell may indicate remaining cyanide; cook it more.

quiz.q: Why should you keep children away from raw cassava and peelings?
options: A) They might eat them and get sick
B) They might make a mess
D) They might use them for play
quiz.explanation: Raw cassava and peelings contain cyanide and can be poisonous if eaten.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to dispose of cassava peelings?
quiz.explanation: Burning or burying deep prevents accidental consumption and environmental harm.

quiz.q: After handling raw cassava, what should you do before touching other foods?
options: B) Wash hands with soap and water
quiz.explanation: Washing with soap and water removes cyanide residue and prevents contamination.
